speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The attacks in Ankara and Brussels are still fresh in our minds.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Closer to home, a quick look at Malaysia, Indonesia and even ourselves, shows that the threat of domestic terrorism is real.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The threats that Singapore faces are ever-changing, and our Home Team and SAF need to stay ahead of the curve to ensure that it is always, and they are always, prepared to deal with any threat of terrorism decisively.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, how does the Ministry plan to transform and optimise its resources and workforce, including Home Team officers, National Servicemen (NSFs) and NSmen to meet these challenges?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, the Home Team also needs to provide the everyday services that we have come to expect and often taken for granted – the key role they play in protecting our communities, ensuring low crime rates, providing efficient and speedy responses in situations of emergencies and keeping our border secure.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Surely, fulfilling all of these responsibilities will require more resources and manpower.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At present, I believe the biggest challenge facing our Home Team is how it will be able to provide a decisive and expedient response to terrorism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order to effectively deal with the threat of terrorism on our shores and in the region, we need to have a strong and muscular response to these threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While deterrence and detection are important pre-emptive tools in our arsenal that must be deployed to combat the threat of terrorism, we must be ready to decisively and resolutely deal with any threat of terrorism that might take place.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this vein, our muscular response as a nation must be three-fold.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, we must possess strong and decisive security forces that are able to protect Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, we must have a pro-active citizenry that is aware and vigilant of impending threats and that is ready to respond to these threats, united as a nation when threats manifest.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, our security agencies must also continue to work closely with regional and international partners to effectively combat terrorism in the region and on a global scale.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order to prepare Singapore to respond to any impending terrorist threat, the Government has conducted realistic, counter-terrorism exercises to stress-test how local authorities and the public would react and respond.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On this note, could the Minister highlight some key learning points from the conduct of these exercises and share further areas of improvement that could make our security forces more effective?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe that SG Future must also be a platform for the Ministry to involve volunteers and community partners in its efforts to keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is ultimately a whole-of-Singapore effort to counter the threat of terrorism as it is both our individual and shared responsibility to work hand-in-hand with the Government, local authorities and all Singaporeans to keep Singapore safe.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we need to start educating people from young, and throughout life, including in our schools.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Building social cohesion, racial and religious harmony and understanding − because values are caught, not just taught.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Awareness of the environment: teaching everyone that security is never "somebody else's problem".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If we see something suspicious, we have to let the authorities know.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And also, emergency preparedness: important that we educate the public on what to do in an emergency.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At a basic level, this can be taught in schools, with progressively more detailed teaching as students grow up.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I look forward to hearing the Ministry's inputs and plans on these issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Minister for Home Affairs had said that it is no longer a question of whether an attack will take place but when an attack will take place in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Such a firm and ominous statement is necessary to spark vigilance in the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But aside from vigilance, there also needs to be strong bonds and trust so that vigilance does not develop into unwarranted suspicion and discrimination or, worse, resentment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate that the Ministry has enhanced strategy and measures to counter these terror threats.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One unfortunate by-product of terror attacks that we have seen happen in other countries is Islamophobia.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think the fear that Islamophobia will creep into our community is real.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have faith that, in general, the non-Muslim community in Singapore knows that Singaporean Muslims strongly reject terrorism and the misguided ISIS actions and, hence, have no reason to distrust or be resentful of Muslims here.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But there may be some who have unspoken doubts or questions about Islam and Muslims and, as the Minister has previously highlighted, people may be too politically correct to express their thoughts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The concern is that if we let these sentiments fester, it may grow into resentment and distrust.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And some extreme few 	Page: 47 may take their feelings too far.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The community can rally efforts to have candid but respectful discussions to build relations amongst people from different races and religions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Currently, there are building safety codes as well as requirements by the Fire Safety Bureau.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: But can MHA, via appropriate legislation or regulations, mandate regular security and threat assessments and audits of such commercial premises and properties so that both safety and security are looked into?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As quickly as Al Qaeda affiliates, such as Jemaah Islamiyah, faded from the public eye in the decade or so after 9/11 and after the death of Osama bin Laden, the place appears to have been taken over by ISIS-inspired ideologues with shocking rapidity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is known that some individuals from Singapore, even our neighbouring countries, have sought to join ISIS in the Middle East and a lot of effort has been put in by Singapore to prevent not just its nationals, but Indonesian citizens, for example, from transiting through our borders to potentially join ISIS ranks.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike the Jemaah Islamiyah movement, there appears to be different opinions with regard to the level of threat posed by ISIS in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An RSIS commentary last year also reported that about 30 different Southeast Asian groups have pledged allegiance to ISIS.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Executive Director of the International Institute for Strategic Studies which organises the Shangri-La Dialogue in a recent Jane's Defence Weekly article was quoted to have said the threat of Katibah Nusantara seeking territory in Southeast Asia was exaggerated, even if there is some danger nonetheless.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, Katibah Nusantara does not appear in the media and in the public consciousness as often as Jemaah Islamiyah did previously.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How can Singaporeans be inoculated against the deviant teachings of such groups?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Has there been a requirement to increase the resources and manpower allocated to MHA as a result of this new wave of terrorism?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the Home Team has a desired outcome of a safe and secure society where lives and property are protected.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It does not tell us about crimes that were not reported and it has been found in other countries that reporting rates are especially low for sexual assault and crimes committed by someone the victim knew well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Vulnerable groups, such as foreign workers, victims of domestic abuse and others, may be reluctant to seek Police help due to fear of repatriation, retaliation or distrust of the Police.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Official crime rates are also influenced by how the Police may reclassify cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, crime rates cannot be attributed to the Police alone.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While Police action can reduce certain types of crime, other crimes are not preventable by Police actions and are a product of social and economic forces.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is done in other countries through national victimisation surveys, such as the British Crime Survey, where the population is asked about their experience with crime.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a population survey should also cover why the crime victims did not report to the Police, thus helping the Police address any service gaps.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another desired outcome of the Ministry is secure borders with efficient and legitimate flow of people, goods and conveyances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under this outcome, the stated KPIs all relate to the legitimacy of inflows, for example, the number of offences detected and unauthorised vessels intercepted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are no measures for the efficiency of flows.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Would the Ministry be brave enough to introduce a measure of efficiency, for example, set a desired time limit within which to process an individual or vehicle through Woodlands or Tuas Checkpoint?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One final desired outcome to highlight is the secure and humane custody of prisoners.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Again, the indicators emphasised on the security aspect only, for example, number of escapes, number of assault cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What about measuring humane custody, which is equally important?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move on to manpower for security and enforcement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My cut is on manpower not just in our law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It also covers the Auxiliary Police and civilian personnel doing law enforcement on behalf of some statutory boards, such as Land Transport Authority (LTA) and Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As far as our State law enforcement agencies are concerned, much has already been said in recent years about the challenges faced by the Singapore Police Force (SPF).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Page: 49 What about the other law enforcement agencies, such as the Singapore Civil Defence Force, Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) and the Singapore Prison Service?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Do they face similar manpower challenges and how are they coping with them?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move on to the Auxiliary Police Forces, particularly CERTIS CISCO and AETOS, who are deployed islandwide.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For this industry, only Singaporeans, Permanent Residents and Malaysians are eligible to apply.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In our daily encounters with Auxiliary Police, we see a large presence of Malaysians in CERTIS and AETOS uniforms.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During the Little India riot, quite a number of Auxiliary Police at the scene were Malaysians.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is the current proportion of Malaysians out of the total Police strength in these two Auxiliary Police Forces?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does the Government have any guidelines on the ratio of Malaysians to Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are there guidelines on any duty or assignments which must be done only by Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, at the immigration checkpoints, are there Malaysians checking their fellow Malaysians, and what would the risk there be?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, I come to the civilian personnel being recruited to do law enforcement on behalf of certain statutory boards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I understand that CERTIS CISCO is the outsourced agent to do enforcement of traffic violations on behalf of LTA and URA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: CERTIS has been recruiting many civilians for such tasks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Recently, I came across one such recruit, an elderly gentleman around 60 and not in good health.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to him, he attended the recruitment interview and specifically requested that he be posted to do enforcement only for URA carpark violations as he assessed that there was less risk of confrontation with members of the public as compared with LTA traffic violations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To his surprise, the next day, he was deployed to a team to do enforcement of LTA violations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: His worst fears were realised when there was, indeed, a confrontation with an irate motorist booked by his team who apparently chased after the enforcement team to dispute the booking.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The gentleman was so traumatised by the incident that he did not return to work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even though such law enforcement has been outsourced to CERTIS, these civilians are exercising law enforcement powers and will affect the public.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The pervasive use of technology has enabled workers of many industries to be productive over a longer period of time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, CCTVs have extended our Police officers' abilities to conduct surveillance over a broader area, which was not previously possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The new security fields, such as cybersecurity and digital forensics, require technical expertise rather than physical conditioning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They polish their craft over time and they get better with age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, intelligence and immigration officers, critical in our fight against 	Page: 50 terrorism, develop ground networks and intuition in picking up would-be threats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These skills cannot be adequately institutionalised and are not easily transferable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As an ex-Police officer of 14 years, we solved many cases because of the wisdom of my ground officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore has extended our retirement and re-employment age because Singaporeans are healthy and productive even when they are older.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Re-employment can also be extended to age 62.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This would ameliorate the Home Team's manpower constraints while retaining core expertise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I personally know many proud Home Team men and women who have dedicated their lives to serving Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, when the time comes for them to retire, 55 or 60 years old is often too late to start a new career.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, our officers are marrying later and their children would only be in their late teens by their retirement age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would Home Team face a leakage of talent as officers seek a longer career in other professions?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Regardless of job scope, physical conditioning and competency should decide their suitability to continue rather than a hard age-cap of 55 years old.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister what is the percentage of officers offered re-employment and what are the reasons some are not offered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I would also like to know how many retired officers have the Home Team helped to find new employment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, how can we tap on our retired officers to continue the mission of defending our homeland?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this complex security climate where terrorism is a constant threat, we need to build a stronger and more integrated Home Team to tackle any security concerns Singapore faces.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There has been a slower pace of recruitment in the last 10 years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will that target now be revised with the increased security risk that we face?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What plans does the Ministry have to ensure that we continue to attract members of the public to join the Home Team and ensure that we have sufficient Home Team staff members to carry out an increasing amount of work?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The following decade saw a decline in birth rates and the number of babies born each year has remained low since.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These cohorts would soon be enlisted for National Service in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Page: 51 Full-time Police National Servicemen (PNSFs) play an important role in the day-to-day police operations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are deployed to man the Neighbourhood Police Centres and Neighbourhood Police Posts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They also conduct frontline patrols in our neighbourhoods and our public transport system, together with their Regular colleagues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These PNSFs serve a critical function in our national security and safety, more so in today's security climate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What measures will the police take to ensure that the level of safety and security will not be compromised by this reduction in headcount?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: However, with the tight labour market situation, I have four suggestions to make to alleviate this challenge.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I say this because there are officers I have spoken to who are eager to carry on but not given re-employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: These officers can perform a variety of roles, from investigation to intelligence work, as they are already trained and have experience.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Third, we can further enhance the productivity and effectiveness of the private security sector as they are the additional eyes and ears on the ground.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can we mandate the use of technology, analytics and biometrics, and MHA grant them full funding support to roll these out.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Fourth, given the nature of recent terrorist attacks and the difficulty in detecting lone wolves and, since both public and private organisations collate data, can the Government tap on such existing data platforms to enhance intelligence operations and investigations to tackle terrorism and heighten and increase productivity?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Png Eng Huat, you have three cuts.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The ills of gambling addiction are well documented.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: More often than not, the people who suffer the most are the family members, not the problem gamblers.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This is made evident by the rising number of Family Exclusion orders issued for the two casinos.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Such orders are initiated by family members to exclude a gambler in their family from the casinos if the gambler is unwilling to address his or her own addiction.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As more families are grappling with problem gambling, it does not make sense to see gambling outlets sprouting up in easy-to-access and family-oriented clubs at the same time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: You drop off 	Page: 52 your children for classes and go meet lady luck at the same location.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In a parliamentary reply in 2000 on the proliferation of betting outlets, the then Finance Minister said, "The locations selected are reasonably far away from places where children will gather − schools, places of worship and so forth.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Singapore Pools will exercise due care and not to place outlets at places where children might be attracted to." If Singapore Pools is concerned about children getting exposed to betting activities at a tender age, should the clubhouses not be concerned, too?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In the same reply, the Minister added that such an offence is typically committed in furtherance of other criminal offences.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This is bad news for some new home owners.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They will find out the hard way when threatening letters, hell notes, paint and graffiti start to appear at the doorstep of their house after they have moved in.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Although the House was told that ICA does work with HDB to inform property owners of the need for timely update of addresses during property sale transactions, I would like to propose that sellers must update their NRIC by the final appointment date or within seven days after that date to complete the sale of their flats.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For sellers who are still homeless at that point in time, I would like to propose that ICA accept personal representation by friends and relatives who are willing to house these sellers as evidence for reporting of change of address.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This will allow the sellers to update their NRIC without the required documentation and complete the sale of their flats without further delay.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of these residents would have lived through those tumultuous years of nation-building.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Many would have worked and contributed to the economy, and some of their children would have attended public schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: A good number of these residents still live in public rental flats.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of them may belong to the Pioneer Generation as well, if only the colour of their identification card were pink.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Page: 53 Last year was our Jubilee Year and I wonder how these stateless people felt living in a country that does not recognise them as citizens despite some of them having lived here for as long as our nation has existed.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As SG50 came to a close, I was reminded of the stateless people I met in 2015.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: He told me his parents and siblings are all Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: He also said he has been receiving assistance from CDC since early 2000.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Another father and daughter remain stateless in 2015 despite the father having worked for the Government and was allowed to buy a flat in the early days, according to the daughter.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: She said her entire family was born in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of the stateless residents have lived here all their lives.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of their children or siblings have become citizens as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I asked a resident if it matters for his ageing mother, who is stateless, to become a citizen after all these years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Over the years, I have personally met several residents in my constituency in Ulu Pandan who were born in Singapore, grew up here, were educated here, worked here, but have yet to be given Singapore citizenship.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Instead, they are recorded as being stateless persons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A common theme that I have found among these individuals is that, often, it was their parents who did not register them for a birth certificate in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Similarly, a recent news report recounted the experiences of a woman born and raised in Singapore who is a stateless person.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In the report, she shared the many struggles that she has faced as a stateless person in Singapore, particularly in her working life, as well as in her personal relationships.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Indeed, being a stateless person must be a difficult and disheartening experience.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Imagine being born in Singapore and having grown up alongside other Singaporeans who are no different from yourself.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Yet, you cannot call yourself a Singaporean nor are you entitled to the privileges that a Singapore Citizen would be entitled to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I would have thought that these individuals, born and bred in Singapore, are more deserving of consideration for Singapore citizenship, as compared to new citizens.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: He highlighted that many of these individuals have come from other countries to live and work in Singapore for long periods of time and had lost their foreign citizenship.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Others were born in Singapore but were not eligible for Singapore citizenship at birth as their parents were not Singapore citizens at the time of their birth and did not obtain foreign citizenship for them from their home countries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As a result, they are considered stateless 	Page: 54 and are without a country to call their own.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These individuals have grown up in Singapore, often having lived their whole lives here, yet they remain unrecognised as Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Many of these stateless individuals are Singaporeans all but in name.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In light of this, would the Minister consider taking a compassionate view regarding these individuals by reviewing the criteria and process for stateless persons who were born in Singapore or who have lived for a significant portion of their lives in Singapore to obtain Singapore citizenship?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: While proper safeguards must be put in place to prevent any abuse of the process, I believe that compassion and acceptance must go hand-in-hand with pragmatism in ensuring that our own are not neglected or forgotten.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Prisoners, first, have to adapt themselves to prison life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This involves stressful and difficult adjustments to a strict institutional routine, deprivation of privacy and living in sparse conditions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: After the initial phase, prisoners often undergo a personal transformation to adapt to prison life which carries traits, such as hyper-vigilance, over-controlling one's emotions to avoid showing vulnerability, such as social withdrawal and isolation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: On a personal level, prisoners may feel guilt and helplessness towards their families and it is not uncommon to see divorce papers being served on inmates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Singapore Prison Service has committed itself to being captains of lives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: They are doing an admirable and difficult job and should be well supported.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: As prisoners are incarcerated as punishment and not for punishment, their stay in jail should, as far as possible, be spent constructively for rehabilitation and eventual release and reintegration into society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The first, on psychological support for inmates, and, second, on inmates' use of time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: What is the policy or approach towards the mental health needs of inmates, whether dealing with pre-existing conditions or issues developed during incarceration?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: What sort of mental health professionals work full time in our prisons?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Is there a ratio of mental health professionals to inmates?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Do the prison officers who manage inmates have compulsory training in mental health issues?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: There has been an IMH Singapore Prison Service Psychiatric Housing Unit set up since 2011.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And are there patients with pre-existing mental conditions or mental needs that developed during incarceration?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Similarly, the number of inmates engaged in work programmes also dropped by 180 from 2014 to 2015.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First, what is the status of the other 19% of inmates?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Second, how were inmates selected for training and work programmes?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Third, how is the employability of inmates determined?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Fourth, what other programmes are in place for inmates who are considered unemployable, to keep them meaningfully occupied?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When someone who has served his/her debt to society for a crime goes on to re-offend, not only is it a loss to that person and his/her family members and friends, but it is also a loss to society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That re-offender could have become a productive contributor to our economy and society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Singapore, we have examples of ex-offenders who have become entrepreneurs, professionals and even religious leaders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The idea of a social impact bond can be summarised as follows, at the risk of some oversimplification.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Investors put up money to buy the bond.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The bond stipulates that a certain social impact target must be met after some years by an NGO or NGO-coalition, perhaps working in concert with public sector partners.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If at the end of the bond period the target is met, the Government redeems the bond.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, then the investors lose their investment and their investment becomes akin to a donation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the goal is reached, the state ensures that its funds are impactful and well spent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Anti-recidivism is a popular subject for social impact bonds because the social impact and the cost to the state can be measured very clearly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, the very first social impact launched by the British government in 2010 was for prisoner rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a move could also spark more interest in and acceptance of social impact bonds in Singapore, which would benefit the social landscape here and help unlock more innovative and result-focused approaches in tackling social challenges.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For repeat offenders, there is impact not only on the drug offenders, but also their family members who have already suffered previously.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There is a tremendous emotional and financial strain on the spouse and the children of drug offenders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I have seen a few cases now in Nee Soon East and some have been arrested and sent back to the Drug Rehabilitation Centres (DRCs) more than twice now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will additional resources be provided to the Singapore Corporation of Rehabilitative Enterprises (SCORE) to expand and increase their efforts?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is often said that when a person is released from prison, they enter another prison.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is because while they might be free from the physical state of imprisonment, the released person still faces the "second prison" of discrimination and being ostracised in society, possibly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This discrimination, more often than not, leads to them not being able to break free of the vicious cycle of crime or to become gainfully employed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Indeed, over the years, the Government has taken several progressive steps to help released persons to reintegrate back into society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: On this note, could the Minister elaborate on whether there are any new programmes or initiatives that will be introduced to help released persons to reintegrate back into society?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: While existing measures have tried to bridge the gap and help released persons break free of the cycle of re-offending, more can still be done to help them to become gainfully employed as part of their reintegration into society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The discrimination that these individuals face from society when they are unemployed or are unable to obtain employment can be detrimental to their rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In fact, this may serve to undermine any progress that they might have made after being released and could actually push them towards re-offending.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In light of this, to help these individuals break free − and assuming they want to break free − of the cycle of re-offending, today, I ask the Government whether it will lead the way in providing employment opportunities for released persons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They could do so by employing released persons in non-sensitive positions within the Civil Service, on a probationary basis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Would the Minister consider this worthy proposal to provide a much needed boost to these released persons?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And should the released person show himself or herself to be a trustworthy and diligent individual, would the Government confirm him as an employee?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This will provide them with an avenue to redeem themselves, give them a sense of self-esteem and also serve as an incentive for them to turn over a new leaf and reduce recidivism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I firmly believe that we must continue to build a passionate society here in Singapore that seeks to welcome back our brothers and sisters who are on that arduous journey of rehabilitation and reconciliation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And we must recognise that an important milestone along that journey is providing them with the opportunity to become gainfully employed and to be able to support themselves and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If a released person is willing to make amends for his mistakes and is ready to turn over a new leaf, we, as a community, must be ready to support them in their rehabilitation, assist in their reintegration into society and welcome them back into the community fold with warm and open 	Page: 57 arms.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Different inmates spend different periods of time incarcerated and, as such, different employment facilitation and skills acquisition strategies are needed to better place them in meaningful employment when they are released from prison or DRCs.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, you have two cuts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: A fair and just society is one that offers second chances, so that Singaporean brothers and sisters who stumble and fall can have the chance to pick themselves up.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Just as it takes a village to raise a child, it takes a community to integrate an ex-offender back into society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: And finding work and stable employment is key to this rehabilitation journey.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: I have met residents in my constituency who were previously incarcerated.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Upon being released, their first instinct was to look for jobs in the security industry, based on recommendations from friends, and perceptions of their prospects.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: But we can imagine that this was not always feasible.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Can it be more closely integrated with skills training and SkillsFuture to expand employment opportunities for ex-offenders who remain our Singaporean brothers and sisters?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Moving upstream, Mdm Speaker, to another scourge − drugs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: We see globalisation is not just about goods and services.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Value systems can be exported to Singapore from halfway around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Nowadays, Singaporeans increasingly have opportunities to study overseas and they can be exposed to new cultures.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Some of it is positive, learning from other countries.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: But we also see some young students being exposed to overseas drug culture.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: The Home Team must continue stepping up education efforts at all levels, especially in our schools, so that young Singaporeans can be further inoculated against the globalisation of the drug culture.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Youths who abuse heroin often do not fully understand the damage they are 	Page: 58 inflicting on themselves. "Ice" appears deceptively harmless as it has short-term upsides with delayed, long-term damage to the abuser.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Upon consumption, ice acts as a stimulant and causes the user to feel more energetic.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Young drug abusers use "ice" as a party drug, to improve performance in studies or sports and to lose weight.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, "ice" has debilitating long-term effects, such as liver, brain and heart damage, leading to strokes and even death.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such attitudes could have been influenced by the legalisation of marijuana in several states in the US for medical and recreational use.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, Singapore has always had a zero-tolerance attitude towards drugs and I believe that we should continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share with us what are the specific reasons for the rising number of youth abusers in Singapore —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan, can you please conclude your speech?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: — and the preventive measures that CNB is putting in place to reach out to our youths?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: I would also like to know if the CNB has any other plans to address the issue.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Counsellors noted a trend of growing acceptance amongst youths towards cannabis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Currently, if a youth is arrested for drug abuse, he will be placed in drug rehabilitation programmes that last up to 36 months.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Apart from preparing an online anti-drug toolkit for educators and parents, how would CNB take the anti-drug battle online and in a more targeted fashion?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Could the authorities work with youth groups, grassroots leaders and entertainment outlet operators to extend our outreach to spread awareness of the danger of cannabis abuse?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Would CNB also need to enhance its capabilities to reverse this trend?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Our tough drug laws have kept Singapore largely free of drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: More importantly, Singapore's zero-tolerance approach towards drugs has contributed towards keeping crime low and has been effective in deterring organised drug syndicates from operating in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: However, more can still be done to further reduce the demand for drugs in Singapore, especially among our youth.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Incarceration in DRCs and deterrent punishments are important, but I also believe that if we are able to stem the use of drugs through effective rehabilitation while in DRC, we would be able to reduce the demand for drugs and, ultimately, reduce the number of drug abusers in Singapore in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Effective rehabilitation can be achieved by ensuring that DRCs are places where inmates are provided with counselling and psychological intervention and are encouraged to find healthy pursuits, such as exercise, reading and vocational training, to replace and usurp the "memory zone" of drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Furthermore, families play a crucial role in helping these inmates not to return to drugs upon their release.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Perhaps DRCs could do more to teach families how to distract inmates post-release, so that they have little time or room to yearn for drugs and relapse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Yes, we need tough laws; yes, we need deterrence; yes, we need incarceration.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But in order to reduce recidivism in earnest, we need genuine efforts to facilitate rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Not "go through motion" efforts but sincere, long-term efforts to rehabilitate those that might have gone astray.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These rehabilitative efforts can be done in DRCs as well as post-release.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This has been attributed to inaccurate information being circulated on social media, as well as the increasing number of states in the United States that have legalised cannabis for so-called "medical" and recreational use.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In light of this, would the Minister provide an update on the effectiveness of on-going preventive drug education efforts by CNB to correct misconceptions about cannabis abuse and to reiterate Singapore's zero-tolerance stance towards drugs?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Further, could the Minister outline what steps are being taken to reverse this troubling increase in the number of cannabis and young cannabis abusers in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If there is a concerted and united effort from all Singaporeans to work towards a drug-free Singapore, we will be able to win the fight against drugs; an on-going war.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: After all, reducing drug recidivism means another life saved – another husband, wife or child saved; a reduction of demand for the drugs and, ultimately, a lower supply of drugs into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In recent years, the nature of crime in Singapore has evolved and changed dramatically.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With Singapore's high Internet and mobile penetration rates, cybercrime has been on a steady rise.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We are witnessing a worrying trend towards more Singaporeans, especially the elderly, falling victim to online scams and cybercrime as syndicates and individuals continue to exploit the speed, convenience and anonymity of the Internet to commit these crimes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is likely that these changes will continue in the years to come; as such, there is a need for the Home Team to adapt to these changes quickly and to have tools to effectively deal with this threat head-on.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In light of this, could the Minister outline what steps have been, or are being taken, to adapt our Home Team to deal with the growing threat of cybercrime in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Furthermore, could the Minister outline what more can be done to raise awareness among the community about the dangers of cybercrime, especially among the youth and the elderly who tend to be more vulnerable to such crimes?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As the nature of crime continues to evolve in Singapore, cybersecurity is also an emerging concern.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Around the world, both governments and the private sector have been the target of cyberattacks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As a result, sensitive personal and corporate information have been stolen and infiltrated systems damaged due to cybersecurity attacks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In January 2016, the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) announced that a new Cyber Security Bill would be introduced to enhance the powers of the Cyber Security Agency.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Could the Minister provide an update on when this Bill will be introduced, and what measures will be included in the Bill to address the growing threat of cybercrimes and cyberattacks in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Lastly, due to the nature of cybercrime, there has also been a shift towards crime becoming increasingly cross-border in nature.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Criminal masterminds can hide outside our borders while making use of local henchmen to take advantage of unsuspecting Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: So, we should continue stepping up Home Team co-operation with their counterparts overseas to improve information sharing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: We also need to continue educating our fellow Singaporeans on how to protect themselves from cybercrime.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: More are learning how to use smartphones and smartphone applications that allow them to communicate with friends and strangers near and afar.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: But it also means that more seniors are becoming vulnerable to targeting by scams and cybercrime.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: I look forward to hearing the Ministry's proposed responses to this emerging challenge.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Page: 61 This is a worrying trend that requires immediate attention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Would the Ministry also consider working with the Ministry of Education (MOE) and People's Association to extend its outreach?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I would also like to ask the Minister, how would the Ministry enhance the capabilities of the Police to effectively enforce against the perpetrators?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Melvin Yong and I are the local Members of Parliament taking care of the residents of Little India.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We wish to speak on behalf of our residents to ensure that the Little India riot of December 2013 will not happen again, the riot being the worst public disorder in Singapore in more than 40 years.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We are thankful for the post-riot recommendations of the Committee of Inquiry (COI) regarding alcohol restrictions, beefing up of Police operations and patrols and the decentralisation of crowds to recreation centres in the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Recently, I was at Little India with Home Affairs Minister Shanmugam and members of the Police Force.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It was obvious that the pre-riot crowds have returned to Little India.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is important that we do not take our eyes off this matter, lest we want history to repeat itself.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The contributions of the foreign workers benefit our entire nation as they help build much of our nation's infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need them and we accept that foreign workers, like the rest of us, have social and leisure needs, amongst other needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The issue is not a Little India locality issue.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a national issue that can only be solved by carefully balancing the needs of all stakeholders – the workers, residents, businesses and the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many 	Page: 62 of these heavy trucks carry soil, sand and other debris heading towards the staging site located behind Fort Road.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Unfortunately, these heavy vehicles travel at fast speeds and do not keep to their lanes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have personally seen on several occasions how they speed and how they occupy all three lanes along the road.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Such driving behaviour poses a danger to other road users, especially when the vehicles are heavy trucks.

text: Residents also complain that on many occasions, the heavy vehicles are not properly covered.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As a result, the roads become dirty due to soil falling off from the trucks.

text: Despite my many appeals to Traffic Police to carry out enforcement, the traffic situation, unfortunately, has not improved.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For cars which are speeding or racing, can we install speed cameras to deter speeding which is dangerous for all road users?

text: Besides school zones, enforcement rounds, education efforts, parent volunteers and red regulating and warning strips, what more can SPF, in particular, Traffic Police, do to mitigate the risk and dangers as it is not just schools that are of concern but also roads within close proximity of places where children gather and wander, such as childcare centres, enrichment centres and play facilities?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But despite the challenging environment and the very substantial number of major events, I think what we can say, looking back over the year, is that crime has remained under control.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Road safety, immigration offending and the fire safety situation are all stable.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim made a number of points about KPIs and I thank her for her comments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What the Home Team does on the ground and what is achieved must obviously go beyond what is in the Budget Book.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The KPIs reflect some broad measures which we published.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In addition, we have internal measures, norms, surveys and also references to serious international benchmarks, which help us achieve our aims and provide a framework for measuring performances, which is important.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All of these, taken together, must lead to the answer to a very basic question: what is the trust and public support that the Home Team agencies, Home Team officers enjoy in Singapore?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our most recent safety and security survey was carried out in 2014 and 90% of Singaporeans felt safe in their neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think no Singaporean will really question that because we know whether we feel safe or we do not feel safe in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This was on people's sense of safety in their neighbourhoods and their confidence in the police force.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Nine in 10 respondents in Singapore said they felt safe walking home alone at night.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Again, I think that is reflective of the way we all feel.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Specifically, Ms Lim made the point that there may be some under-reporting of crimes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In particular, I accept that victims of sexual offences may sometimes be unwilling to report and there could be a variety of reasons for this: fear, in a situation of power imbalance, particularly when the victim is young and knows the offender.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I accept that these victims need to be helped.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our sense is that, in general, in terms of the statistics, the under-reporting is unlikely to make a significant difference to what we have set out as the crime statistics, but we must help those who do not report out of fear.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have undertaken another major review of our criminal processes and criminal laws in general.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As I have said before, we do these reviews regularly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A couple of months ago, I asked for such a review to be done.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will ask my officers to consider, in the context of the review, the points made by Ms Lim, including the possibility of surveys to establish the level of under-reporting.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our own sense, as I have said, is that in Singapore, at least, given the levels of education, the concerns about the Police or fears about the system are unlikely to be major reasons for under-reporting, and classification is a matter of assessment, but I think the point is, at this stage, worth looking at.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Lim also asked about measuring checkpoint efficiency.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At our checkpoints, we track efficiency as an internal measure.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is important that we turnaround travellers quickly, for Singaporeans and also because we are an international tourist destination.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, of course, efficiency will not be pursued at the expense of security.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: How we get the balance 	Page: 64 right depends on our assessment of the threats, which can vary from time to time, and the overall general situation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is our own serious assessment based on available information.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, Sidney Jones, Director of Jakarta-based Institute for Policy Analysis of Conflict, said that the January attacks in Jakarta "may be a harbinger of more violence to come" and that ISIS "has already transformed the terrorism threat in Indonesia".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But as Mr Singh pointed out, there are some who have said that the threat is exaggerated.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After Paris, Jakarta and Brussels, all within five months of each other, I think Members will agree we cannot take that approach, that since some experts think that the threat is exaggerated, therefore, we do not have to take the threat seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Returning foreign fighters, such as those from Katibah Nusantara, pose a particular threat, a serious threat.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are battle-hardened with combat skills, violent tendencies and extremist ideology and completely intent on perpetrating violence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Katibah Nusantara issues videos in Malay, aimed squarely at the Malay populations in this region.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Malaysia, in the last year, more than 100 people have been arrested, including commandos, police officers, military officers, civil servants, because of their allegiance to ISIS or terrorist leanings.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At least one plot was disabled a few hours before it was to be carried out, right in the heart of Kuala Lumpur.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some Members have asked how we will deal with this heightened terror threat.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One, strengthen the protection of hard and soft targets and take other measures, including enhancing the video camera network around Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Two, enhance our security response capabilities to respond quickly and effectively to any attack.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Ms Rahayu Mahzam spoke about the need to have a whole-of-society mindset in security and to start young.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The community has always played an important role in keeping Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin will speak more about our partnerships with the community.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will try to take the CEP to a new level.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will seek to empower the community to stay alert, stay united and stay strong in the face of the terrorist threats.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, ultimately, SG Secure cannot just be a public awareness campaign.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will build on what we have achieved through the CEP.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Page: 65 CEP was focused on maintaining and enhancing social cohesion and harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The success depends on the community responding to the call, though we intend to do everything we can to bring it to the community.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will roll out programmes which seek to touch almost every section of our society − on awareness, on responses and on coming together, if there is an attack.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, we have taken action against those who sell ISIS flags.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have taken action against those who propagate ISIS' ideology.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And those who intended to go to fight in conflict zones, we have taken action against them as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our experience, and the global experience, is that radicalisation is a process that can happen without forewarning, and very quickly, in a matter of a month in some cases.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We make an assessment of an individual – his motivations, actions, personality and character.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What danger does he pose to society and to the country?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We need to be alert even to the slightest indication of danger and take action and leave no one in doubt as to where we stand.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Singh said that other countries ‒ I think he mentioned Bangladesh ‒ perhaps had taken a more nuanced view and, indeed, they do.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I want to dwell on this a bit because it is a very important point.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Let us take a few examples of countries which have taken a different approach from us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For years, they allowed hate speech, in the name of civil liberties.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That has contributed to the situation that you have in Belgium today.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am not saying solely, but it certainly has contributed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Other reasons – you have ghettos, you have significant under-employment or unemployment – but the key is the spread of ideology, free and unfettered, in a permissive environment because many of those who get involved are not unemployed, they are highly-educated and well-employed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you then turn to the UK ‒ and I want to refer to this article – not so much to assert the truth of it from the BBC but more to indicate if we had such a situation ‒ how would we deal with it?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Almost like, if I were to give you a situation, how would Singapore deal with it?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is about a gentleman by the name of Masood Azhar, a Pakistani.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was a VIP guest of Britain's leading Islamic scholars.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He went to Britain in 1993 for a lecture, and I quote, "When one of the world's most important jihadist leaders landed at Heathrow Airport on 6 August 1993, a group of Islamic scholars from Britain's largest mosque network was there to welcome him.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Today, he is wanted by the Indian authorities following the attack on the Pathankot military base in January this year." A BBC investigation revealed an astounding insight into the way in which hardcore jihadist ideology was promoted in some mainstream UK mosques in the early 1990s and involved some of Britain's most senior Islamic scholars.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He addressed the students and teachers, telling them that a substantial proportion of the Koran had been devoted to "killing for the sake of Allah" and that a substantial volume of sayings of the Prophet Muhammad were on the issue of jihad.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He spoke on "the divine promise of victory to those engaged in jihad".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And he told students, "You should prepare for jihad without any delay, you should get jihadist training from wherever you can and we are also ready to offer our services" and so on and so forth.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If such a person came to Singapore, first of all, he would have been prevented from 	Page: 66 coming to Singapore; and, second, if he said those things here, he would be arrested and deported.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If a Singaporean said these things, he would be advised not to say them and, if he continued, he would be detained.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They were not thinking of doing it in Singapore, they were discussing it generally.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There can be a time gap between thinking about these things and actually carrying them out somewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Bangladesh was prepared to put 13 of them on surveillance while detaining the others.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The question is whether we allow them to stay or ask them to leave.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it is different question from Bangladesh which has got to deal with its own citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Do we, say, 13 of them, we put on some sort of surveillance and expend our resources, or do we ask all 27 to leave?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think the acid test will be this question if I were to pose it to Members, "How many of your residents will be happy if I put 13 of them in foreign workers' dorms in your constituency?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Would you rather have them in Singapore or out of Singapore?" I think those are the questions for us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, they are free to move around but with some restrictions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We treat our citizens differently but, when they are foreign workers, we ask them to leave for obvious reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if we look at Indonesia, for example, again, the differences in approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Four Indonesians recently came through, including a 15-year-old boy.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: ICA did it quite well, we picked them up and we realised that they were going to go off to the Middle East to fight.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we handed them over to the Indonesian authorities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Singapore, they would have been subjected to the Internal Security Act.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are free to go around, thinking of more things to do and, perhaps, making further attempts to get to the Middle East.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The reason I have set out our position quite comprehensively on this is that we need to be guided by our assessment of what is and is not safe for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If other countries wish to treat would-be terrorists in a different way, they do so taking the consequences of their decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, two of the suicide bombers who took part in the recent Jakarta attacks had just been released from prison.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because a release before rehabilitation means that they may perpetrate more crimes and, in Indonesia, the cost of their decision to release was the blood of innocents.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It does not mean that when we release, we can always be absolutely sure that the person will not get back to his ways.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is always a risk, but, at least, we do not need to release until we have made that assessment.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I agree with Ms Rahayu Mahzam that we also have to exercise sensitivity in the way we do the messaging, making it clear that our fight is against extremism and violence and not against any particular race, ethnicity or religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Indeed, the Government, through my speeches as well as the speeches of others, has made that absolutely plain.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And, in fact, we have emphasised the responsibility that the majority in Singapore have to make sure that there is social cohesion, 	Page: 67 harmony and peace.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to make it clear that our fight is against extremism and violence and not against any particular religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to stay united, instead of being divided.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to take a collective stand against those who threaten our harmony and way of life and do all we can to protect the multi-racial and multi-religious soul of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Patrick Tay spoke about the need to better tap on existing data and platforms to support our counter-terrorism operations.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In this heightened threat environment, we have to use all available resources at our disposal to detect and respond to threats.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These contain important data that can be vital to our safety and security.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We had initially taken the position that some of these data would not be used.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Mah Bow Tan and Dr Yaacob Ibrahim had all said that in the past.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But the changed security environment means that we have to change the position on not using such data.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I wish to state that clearly here, since it is a change from what we had said previously in Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In this changed security environment, the Home Team must be able to collect and analyse suspicious travel patterns and respond swiftly and decisively, for our collective security.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we do not rely on the existing data, then we have to spend taxpayers' money to redo the entire infrastructure to look at how people move because that is one of the ways in which you will now analyse its patterns, apart from other data.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fight against terrorism must begin, must be fought, beyond our borders as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr de Souza pointed out that effective regional and international partnerships are key.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have strong reciprocal intelligence and information exchanges with our foreign counterparts.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have also strengthened legislation to enable quick and effective action against terrorism and terrorism financing, and we have enhanced our international cooperation capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: However, even with our best efforts, we cannot rule out the possibility of an attack in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over the next 10 to 15 years, four major developments will have a profound impact on the complexity and volume of work that the Home Team handles.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This will change a lot of the work that we do.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, emergency ambulance calls have increased by about 5% annually for the past five years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At this rate, the volume of calls will easily double in 15 years and it is likely that it will not grow at a standard 5% rate as our population ages quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, our traveller and cargo volumes are growing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Last year, our land checkpoints handled close to 400,000 travellers per day.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third, the Home Team now has to confront new manifestations of crime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2015, a rise in cybercrime led to an overall rise in the crime rate in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And most of these are committed from abroad.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Given technological advancements, we can expect the volume and complexity of cybercrimes to grow.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Senior Minister of State Desmond Lee will say more about this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are growing and, in some situations, the way some people treat our officers is unacceptable.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have observed an increasing trend of hurt and verbal abuse towards Home Team officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have been threatened, insulted, punched, kicked and bitten.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will take firm action against such abusive persons, including prosecuting them and pressing for stiff sentences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All these factors increase the workload on the Home Team.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There will be limits to how many more ambulance crews, immigration officers or Police officers we can employ.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We would like to have more manpower across the Home Team – to answer Ms Lim's question specifically – whether it is Police, ICA, SCDF, as prison officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The macro situation in Singapore is that there are smaller numbers of younger Singaporeans entering the workforce each year as a result of our birth rates.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the public sector takes more, then the private sector will be squeezed even more.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the Government imposes some caps on the growth of the public sector.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This discipline is necessary, for the sake of the country.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Within the public sector, other Ministries, agencies, also need manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I was in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, I know.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They had difficulties, too, and I spoke about them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, everyone has to live with less manpower than ideal and that is the situation in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the Home Team, we are certainly not in an ideal situation, in terms of manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Given the limited overall manpower pool and, in particular, the stringent requirements of the Home Team, uniformed services, for obvious reasons, the requirements are stringent and strict, both in terms of fitness and character, in terms of our assessment of the person's suitability.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It does not mean we always get it right but there are a number of requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we are not able to get all the manpower that we need.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we will do our best to ensure the safety and security outcomes remain good.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As it is, in a less than ideal situation, with the far fewer number of Home Team officers, Police officers, how are we doing?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Based on statistics, Members can see from the indicators, overall crime rate, dealing with emergencies, our drug situation, I think, on most criteria, we are among the best in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I set this out in some detail because I want to acknowledge the central point that Ms Lim makes about manpower challenges and explain the broad limitations on what we can do about it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But beyond the present, the fact that we are doing okay today, we are doing well today, is no guarantee of the future.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I am focused on the years ahead, how will our challenges develop and how will we respond.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We need an operating model to enhance our operational effectiveness and manage our workload.
